newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Bulgarian students hold torchlight protest.
newsitem.headline: Bulgarian students hold torchlight protest.

text.p: Bulgarian students carrying flaming torches marched through early evening fog in Sofia on Friday to back opposition demands for a general election.
Talks between rival political factions showed no sign of compromise but cracks began to appear in the ruling Socialists' parliamentary majority.

Despite 18 days of opposition street protests and the threat of more serious unrest to come, the Socialists are insisting on forming a new government to replace that of Zhan Videnov, who resigned on December 21.
One Socialist deputy, Alexander Marinov, said he was leaving the party and the Bulgarian Business Bloc said it would not take part in a vote for a new Socialist cabinet.
Two other reformist Socialist deputies have supported the opposition's view that early elections are the only way out of the crisis.
About 2,000 students joined the march and thousands more demonstrators rallied outside the gold-domed Alexander Nevsky cathedral.
"It is clear that no dialogue is possible and we see no reason for further talks," opposition leader Ivan Kostov told the rally. "Victory will be ours."

Political sources said President Petar Stoyanov would try to bring rival factions together again on Sunday while the opposition hoped to woo enough Socialist deputies to ensure the defeat of a vote on a new cabinet.

The constitution requires Stoyanov, who took office on Wednesday, to ask the Socialists as the biggest party in parliament to form a government, but the opposition has threatened mass protests and a general strike if he does so.
Leaders of the two parliamentary groups met together at the presidency for more than two hours but no solution appeared to be in sight.

"Unfortunately, there is a complete difference between the positions and assessments of the United Democratic Forces and the Democratic Left," said Kostov, leader of the main opposition party, the Union of Democratic Forces (UDF).

Socialist Party leader Georgi Parvanov, attempting a more positive interpretation, said they had agreed on the need for economic reforms and for measures to ease social tensions, but his party still insisted on forming the government.
Stoyanov told reporters he had warned against any untenable "Balkan compromise" and said the Socialists' proposal to form a broad-based cabinet of technocrats was unlikely to win popular confidence.
"I asked them to consider the interests of Bulgaria and from this point of view what will happen if they fail," he said.

Bulgaria urgently needs a credible government to negotiate a new accord with the International Monetary Fund, which has suspended disbursements because the Socialist government failed to implement the last reform programme.

In the meantime, the national currency, the lev, closed at new lows of 920-930 to the dollar on the interbank market on expectations on further political instability and the knowledge that the central bank cannot to support it. The bank fixed the currency at 813.87 for Monday, down on Friday's 731.71.
A European Union statement issued by the Dutch embasssy in Sofia expressed deep concern about events in Bulgaria and urged rapid and effective structural reforms.
"The EU encourages all political parties to support the recently-elected president in his endeavour to facilitate compromise solutions including on a date for elections," it said.
